Week 67 Appendix: The Week the Court Opened a Door

A Supreme Court ruling on voting rights collapsed into days of state redistricting, while a shooting became leverage against courts, critics, and the press.

This was a week defined by the convergence of a real security crisis with a preexisting authoritarian playbook, and by a landmark judicial rollback of voting-rights protections. A shooting at the White House Correspondents' Dinner became the pretext for an aggressive, coordinated push to override a federal injunction, pressure a preservation nonprofit to drop its lawsuit, and fast-track legislation funding Trump's contested ballroom—demonstrating governance by manufactured urgency. Simultaneously, the DOJ indicted James Comey a second time over an ambiguous social media post, the FCC threatened ABC's broadcast licenses over a Kimmel joke, and Trump publicly blamed the 'No Kings' protest movement for the assassination attempt against him. The most structurally significant event was the Supreme Court's Louisiana v. Callais decision gutting Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which triggered immediate, explicit state-level moves (Louisiana suspending an active primary, Tennessee and Mississippi targeting Black-majority districts, Florida enacting a new gerrymander) to dilute minority representation before the midterms. Congress simultaneously ended DHS shutdown standoffs while abdicating war-powers oversight of the Iran conflict.

(2026-04-25)
  2. Todd Blanche and DOJ officials demanded the National Trust for Historic Preservation drop its ballroom lawsuit, citing the shooting incident: The Justice Department pressured a private nonprofit to abandon litigation challenging a presidential construction project, using a security incident as leverage against judicial review. (2026-04-25)
  3. DOJ (Todd Blanche) filed a motion to dissolve the court injunction blocking White House ballroom construction: The executive branch sought to overturn a judicial order restraining a presidential project, attacking the plaintiff's legitimacy rather than addressing the underlying legal merits. (2026-04-28)

DOJ filed an emergency motion citing the assassination attempt to argue the ballroom injunction must be lifted: Within 72 hours of an attempted assassination, the administration used the incident to demand a federal court dissolve an injunction on a presidential construction project.
